item.title: Your Similarity Cutoff Deletes the Rules First: Constraint Facts Score Below Descriptions in Local Embedders (2026)
item.description: On a 12-fact fixture with two local Ollama embedders, one of four constraint queries scored 0.660 under all-minilm, below a 0.7 cosine cutoff, while descriptive facts scored 0.764-0.773. The same constraints all clear 0.90 on snowflake-arctic-embed:33m. Method, sweep and a probe you can run.
item.content:encoded:
Your memory pipeline ends with a score gate: keep rows at or above 0.7 cosine similarity, drop the rest. You tuned that number on topical questions and it looked fine. Then someone asks “May I deploy to production on Friday?” and the agent retrieves nothing — not the wrong thing, nothing — because the one stored sentence that should have stopped the deploy scored 0.660.

That is the measurement in this article, scoped to what was actually run. On a 12-fact synthetic fixture with two local Ollama embedders, the prohibition “Deployment to production on Fridays is prohibited for all teams.” scored 0.660 against “May I deploy to production on Friday?” under all-minilm:latest. The two descriptive facts in the same fixture scored 0.764 and 0.773 for their own questions. A 0.7 gate therefore keeps the descriptions and deletes the rule, and the ordering reverses on the second embedder — the same prohibition scores 0.949 under snowflake-arctic-embed:33m. The safe cutoff is a property of the encoder, not of your application.

The fixture is small and this is not an effect size. It is enough to show the effect exists, that it is embedder-dependent, and to justify spending twenty minutes measuring it on your own facts before you trust a threshold you inherited.

What was measured, and what was not

The fixture is 12 facts and 6 queries, committed in the probe script: 6 constraints (two prohibitions, two requirements — who may rotate production keys, and migrations inside the maintenance window — one exception to the deployment freeze requiring engineering-director approval, and one exclusion of contractors from incident command) and 6 descriptive facts over the same entities — backups, on-call rotation, keys, GPU cluster, deployment pipeline, incident reviews. Four of the six queries target a constraint; two target a description. Each query has exactly one gold fact.

Scoring is exact cosine over the full returned vectors, with no ANN index in the loop, so approximate-search recall loss cannot be mistaken for the cutoff effect. The threshold sweep runs 0.20 to 0.90 in 0.05 steps. Both embedders run locally through Ollama’s /api/embed at 384 dimensions (all-minilm:latest, digest 1b226e2802db; snowflake-arctic-embed:33m, digest e8db0186); the harness sends the whole fact list and the whole query list in two batched calls per model, and re-running reproduces every score to three decimals.

Not measured, and not claimed here: an effect size, generality across embedders or corpora, any product’s default cutoff, or the behaviour of any hosted vector database’s approximate index. This article also does not claim that constraint facts are always penalised. It reports the direction found on this fixture and the sweep that exposes it.

Result 1: the constraint is the only row under the gate

Under all-minilm:latest, the six gold scores split in a way that matters:

query  gold  score   rank  best descriptive competitor
q1     c1    0.660   1     d2 0.304   (Friday deployment prohibition)
q2     c2    0.857   1     d3 0.705   (key rotation ownership)
q3     c3    0.900   1     d4 0.411   (PII in notebooks)
q4     c5    0.821   1     d1 0.251   (long migration window)
q5     d1    0.764   1     —          (backups: where and when)
q6     d2    0.773   1     —          (on-call rotation)

Both descriptive gold scores (0.764, 0.773) sit above the constraint score for q1 (0.660). The gold fact is ranked first for all six queries, so this is not a ranking problem — it is a magnitude problem. Cosine similarity for “May I deploy on Friday?” against the rule that forbids it is lower than cosine similarity for “When do backups run?” against the sentence describing backups. Gate at 0.7 and q1 returns zero rows: the gold is 0.660, the next-best fact overall is another constraint (c4) at 0.338, and the best descriptive competitor is 0.304.

Under snowflake-arctic-embed:33m the same texts order the other way: constraints score 0.942 to 0.980, descriptions 0.897 to 0.923. The Friday prohibition scores 0.949. Every constraint gold clears 0.90; the descriptive q5 gold at 0.897 is the one row that falls below that gate.

Result 2: the sweep shows where recall breaks, and it breaks differently per embedder

Constraint recall is the fraction of constraint-targeted queries whose gold fact survives the gate. At 0.70 under all-minilm:latest it is 0.75 — three of four — and overall recall is 0.833.

threshold   all-minilm constraint recall   snowflake-arctic-embed constraint recall
0.20-0.65   1.00                            1.00
0.70        0.75                            1.00
0.75        0.75                            1.00
0.80        0.75                            1.00
0.85        0.50                            1.00
0.90        0.25                            1.00

Nothing changes between 0.20 and 0.65 on either model. The first loss under all-minilm is exactly the q1 score of 0.660 crossing a 0.70 gate; the second loss at 0.85 is q4 at 0.821, and at 0.90 only q3 at 0.900 remains. Under snowflake the constraint set is intact to 0.90; at that threshold the description q5 at 0.897 is what falls out, which is the mirror image of the all-minilm failure.

Two operational consequences follow. First, on these fixtures a cutoff up to 0.65 is safe for both embedders, and the failure is not “thresholds are bad” but “this threshold was never validated against the fact type that matters”. Second, a cutoff copied from a notebook tuned on another encoder is a different number in practice: the same 0.7 that costs one of four constraints under all-minilm costs nothing under snowflake.

Result 3: the failure mode here is an empty retrieval

The planning assumption for this article was that a descriptive fact would outrank the rule and get returned in its place. That is not what happened. Across all 15 thresholds on both embedders, the count of queries where the gold constraint was dropped while a descriptive fact survived above the same gate was zero. On q1 the next-best descriptive fact scored 0.304; the next-best fact overall was c4, another constraint, at 0.338.

That distinction changes the symptom but not the risk. A wrong-but-plausible description at least gives the model something to reason about, and a careful agent may notice the mismatch. Zero rows gives it nothing, and the failure is silent: the prompt simply contains no memory, and the model answers from its prior. Which of these two you get depends on how densely your store covers the query’s topic. If your facts are thick around deployment, you will get substitution; if they are sparse, as here, you get emptiness. Both are the same gate deleting the same row.

Why raising top-k or adding MMR does not fix it

top_k is applied to the candidates that already passed the score filter. Raising it from 5 to 50 changes how many survivors you keep; it cannot restore a row that was removed before ranking. The same applies to MMR or any diversity reranker placed after the filter, and to hybrid search weighted by a vector score that still has to clear the threshold.

The failure sits upstream of every ranking control you have. Either the row clears the gate or it does not, so the only levers that work are (a) lowering the gate, with the precision cost that implies for topical queries, (b) making constraint rows score higher for constraint-shaped questions, or (c) taking constraint rows out of the similarity gate entirely.

There is a secondary trap worth naming: cosine similarity is not one portable number. Qdrant’s collections documentation states that cosine similarity is implemented as a dot product over vectors normalised at upload, so the value you see is only comparable inside a store that documents that normalisation; Chroma’s collection configuration documents that space “defines the distance function of the embedding space” and that its default is squared L2, with cosine and inner product as opt-in alternatives. A 0.7 cutoff moved from a cosine collection to an L2 collection is not the same filter, and a similarity of 0.7 is not a distance of 0.7. Check the metric before you compare scores across stores, and never compare a similarity against a distance threshold.

Measure your own sweep before you pick a number

The probe behind this article is a single file with the fixture inline: threshold_probe.py. It needs a local Ollama and nothing else — no API key, no network beyond 127.0.0.1, no vector database. Replace the FACTS and QUERIES lists with your own rows and mark each fact constraint or description, then run it against whichever model you serve:

python3 threshold_probe.py > probe_results.json

It prints, per embedder, the gold score and rank for every query, the best-scoring descriptive competitor, and constraint recall at each threshold in the sweep. Three numbers are worth reading before you set a gate:

  1. The lowest constraint gold score. Any cutoff above it deletes a rule.
  2. Constraint recall at your current threshold. Below 1.0 means a rule-bearing question already returns nothing.
  3. The gap between your descriptive floor and your constraint floor. If the constraint floor is lower, a gate tuned on descriptions is mis-tuned for rules by construction.

A 6-fact fixture is enough to find your own q1; the run takes seconds. Two caveats about the artifact: it is a fixture-in-code script rather than a library with a CLI, and the two model tags are hard-coded in EMBEDDERS, so you edit those lines to match what your host serves. The published methodology records the host, the model tags, the dimensions and the exact command.

What to do instead

Store polarity as a field, not as a sentence. If a memory row carries kind: constraint with a scope (“production”, “all teams”, “Fridays”), you can retrieve constraints for a query that asks permission with a metadata filter and skip the similarity gate for that subset. This is the fix that survives an encoder swap, because it does not depend on how a particular model scores a modal verb.

Route constraint facts around the gate. Take the top-k by score, then union in all constraint rows that match the query’s entities, then rank. The gate’s job — removing noise — is preserved for the open-ended recall path where it was tuned.

Pin the cutoff per embedder, after measuring. If you keep a single numeric gate, derive it from the sweep rather than from a tutorial, and re-derive it when the encoder or its version changes. On this fixture the defensible statement is that a gate at or below 0.65 lost nothing under either embedder; every number above that is a claim requiring its own measurement. Scores are encoder-specific and, as the version pin in any model card suggests, encoder-version-specific too — the same reasoning as swapping encoders on an existing store, where the vectors, not just the cutoff, change meaning.

Do not delete the gate to solve this. Without it, a top-k over a large store returns weak matches for every query and the prompt fills with noise. The finding is that one number cannot serve both fact types, not that filtering is wrong.

Limitations and what would falsify this

The fixture is 12 facts and 6 queries with four constraint queries, on one host, on one day, with two local 384-dimension embedders. Four of six queries target constraints, so the constraint median is not a population estimate. The article reports this run’s numbers only; an earlier 8-fact planning probe reported a different descriptive-survivor pattern, and that pattern is not what this fixture produced, so it is not repeated here as a finding. ANN-index behaviour is out of scope by design: exact cosine was used precisely so that approximation error could not be confused with the cutoff.

Three results would overturn the practical recommendation. If constraint recall tracks descriptive recall across the whole sweep on both embedders for your corpus, then your gate is fine and only the numbers in this article are fixture-specific. If the constraint-versus-description gap closes once facts are embedded as multi-sentence documents rather than single sentences, then the effect is a property of short-fact embedding and should be stated that way. If a reranker placed before the filter recovers the dropped constraint without a score change, then the fix is architectural rather than metadata. Each of these is testable with the same probe and a different fixture.

What is already established by the run: a 0.7 cosine gate deleted one of four rules on this fixture under one embedder and none under another, the deletion was an empty retrieval rather than a wrong answer, and raising top_k cannot undo it. That is a narrow claim, and it is enough to justify checking your own cutoff against your own constraint facts before the next permission question arrives.

Method, fixture hash, per-query scores and the raw sweep are in the probe results, the probe script and the method notes, with file hashes in the manifest. These are first-party files created for this article, containing no customer data and no third-party downloads.

For where this sits in the wider picture, see the agent memory framework comparison for retrieval-quality metrics, the mem0 configuration guide where a similarity threshold appears as a setting without a measured cost, what changes when you swap encoders, the other silent embedder failure at the context ceiling, and what deletion actually removes if you decide to prune rule rows rather than retrieve them.

Primary sources for the store-level claims: Qdrant’s collections documentation on cosine-as-normalised-dot-product, Chroma’s collection configuration docs on the space parameter and its squared-L2 default, and the Ollama model pages for all-minilm and snowflake-arctic-embed for the model families used here.

item.title: Agent Context Compaction: What Gets Lost—and How to Test It
item.description: Published measurements of summarisation loss are narrower and stranger than the advice: temporal expressions survived at 3.05% before a one-sentence prompt fix and 62.39% after, named entities and event structure barely changed, and 5x compression raised retrieval calls from 21.0 to 63.9 while completion stayed flat. This post reads those results, separates them from the model's own recall limits, and ships a 12-probe retention test — probe template, scorer and fixture test — for your own transcripts.
item.content:encoded:
An agent works for two hours. The harness compacts the transcript, the run continues, and somewhere in the next twenty turns it re-runs a migration it has already run, asks the user for a value the user typed an hour ago, or refactors a file it was explicitly told not to touch. Nothing in the run log marks the turn where that fact disappeared. The summary reads fluently, the task still finishes, and the only trace of the loss is work the agent repeats.

That is the reader problem this post takes up: which pinned facts survive a summarisation pass, what the pass costs in tokens, and how to make the facts that cannot be lost survive it. The framing matters, because “which facts survive” is an empirical question and the honest answer is narrower than the advice literature implies. Every number below is quoted from a published study or a vendor document and linked where it appears. No retention figure here is a measurement performed by this article; what the post adds is a reading of the published evidence and the shape of a retention test an operator can run against their own harness.

Three shipped compaction paths, and they lose different things

Compaction is not one mechanism. Anthropic’s production API path replaces older conversation turns with a summary that the model writes on the server, so the client needs no summarisation code of its own (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/compaction). Because the summary is generated rather than selected, its content is not deterministic across runs or model versions. The API summariser’s own prompt and target length are unpublished, and no per-fact measurement of what that summary retains is published either — which is a narrower statement than vendor-wide silence on retention, as the next section shows.

The second path is deletion rather than summarisation. The context-editing API’s clear_tool_uses_20250919 strategy “automatically clears the oldest tool results in chronological order” and replaces each cleared result with placeholder text signalling removal (https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/context-editing). Chronological age is the only criterion, so “oldest” is not “least relevant”: the file listing from turn 3 goes before the wrong hypothesis from turn 30, and a search result that established a fact can vanish while the conclusion drawn from it stays.

The third path is the client harness. Claude Code auto-compacts when a conversation approaches its context limit, accepts per-run preservation instructions through /compact, and treats the resulting cache miss as an expected rebuild, because the rewritten conversation “invalidates the conversation layer: the next request has a new, shorter history that doesn’t share a prefix with the old one” (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching). For this harness the vendor also publishes a mechanism-level survival table: CLAUDE.md and auto memory are re-injected, up to five files are re-read, and skill bodies are re-injected up to 5,000 tokens each with the oldest dropped first (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/context-window#what-survives-compaction). That is not a per-fact retention rate, and it says nothing about the API summariser, but it is the closest thing to a published answer for any single implementation — and it makes the escape hatch concrete. Preservation instructions are a supported input, which makes “pin these facts” a documented affordance rather than a hack.

All three share one property that matters operationally: the compaction event is a rewrite of prior context, not an append. Whatever the pass drops is gone from the window rather than demoted within it.

A passing summary is not evidence of fidelity

The intuitive test — read the summary and see whether it looks right — fails because fluency is exactly what a summariser optimises. Anthropic’s own guidance concedes the difficulty: “the art of compaction lies in the selection of what to keep versus what to discard, as overly aggressive compaction can result in the loss of subtle but critical context whose importance only becomes apparent later” (https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents). The same guidance recommends tuning for recall before precision: a summary that carries a fact you did not need costs tokens, while a summary that omits one costs a wrong action.

Measured work on the failure mode agrees that completion is the wrong dependent variable. In a deterministic planning environment with a fixed 24-turn horizon, 5x compression moved GPT-5.5 completion from 80% to 85% — statistically nothing, p = 1.0 — while retrieval calls rose from 21.0 to 63.9 at p = .002 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16370). Retrieval increased in all six model-regime comparisons, and completion changed significantly only for DeepSeek at 10x compression. The compressed agent finished as often and paid for it in reacquisition: it went back for state the uncompressed agent still had in front of it. The authors also report that the signature is environment-dependent, with ALFWorld showing no such retrieval surge, which is a useful warning against generalising any single ratio.

A second line of work catalogues the qualitative shape of that cost. A preliminary study of verifier-guided compaction reports that compression “can weaken the influence of recent interactions, increasing blocked actions, repeated exploration, and instability across runs” (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06503). The authors label it preliminary and report no per-fact retention rate, so it supports a taxonomy rather than a number: the symptoms are blocked action, repeat exploration and run-to-run variance, and all three are invisible in a completion-rate dashboard.

Which fact classes fail first

The sharpest per-fact evidence comes from a controlled gist-compression study over all ten LoCoMo conversations at temperature 0 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11775). Its question counts and its preservation numbers do not share a denominator, and the paper is explicit about which is which. The study evaluates 1,935 matched text-only questions across the ten conversations, and its primary accuracy aggregate uses the 1,501 that remain once Category 5 (adversarial) questions are excluded. The preservation figures are a separate analysis: Table 3 reports verbatim preservation rates across all ten conversations over the 952 temporal expressions it found, so 3.05% before a one-sentence prompt fix and 62.39% after it are expression-level rates, not question-level accuracies. Named-entity and event preservation rates “barely change (x1.02 and x1.11)”. What the fix moved at question level is judge accuracy on category-2 (temporal) questions: +0.314 [0.254, 0.375], paired over n = 315 questions in the matched set. Both readings describe the same mechanism — the gist abstraction kept who did what to whom and dropped when.

Two things follow. First, the failure is class-specific, not global: the authors trace it to a mechanism — the gist abstraction preserved relational and event structure while omitting when things happened — and they report preservation per content type rather than as one blended rate. A coding agent’s most-reused classes are the ones this study finds fragile on the temporal side — file paths, command strings, version numbers, the exact revision a decision was made against — because those are identifier-shaped values that a prose summary naturally paraphrases into something lossy rather than wrong-looking. Second, the entire difference came from wording: the paper’s improved condition is “identical to SWC-Full except for one added sentence at the prompt start”, and that one sentence took expression-level temporal preservation from 3.05% to 62.39% with no other change to the pipeline. The lever is instruction, not architecture.

Why class matters at all is the older result on position. Performance is “often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end of the input context, and significantly degrades when models must access relevant information in the middle of long contexts” (https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172). Compaction changes where a surviving fact sits: a constraint from the opening turns survives only if the summary places it somewhere the model still attends to, and the middle of a reconstructed summary is the worst place for it. Chroma’s Context Rot report extends the same caution across a modern panel, finding that performance varies significantly with input length even on simple tasks across the 18 models evaluated (https://research.trychroma.com/context-rot) — so a longer, more faithful summary is not automatically a safer one.

The control arm you cannot skip

Any retention test that omits a no-compaction control measures the wrong thing. If the same probes fail on the full transcript, the loss belongs to the model’s recall over 10k tokens, not to the summary, and no compaction fix will help. Two decision rules follow from that, and both are falsifiers rather than heuristics.

If the control arm fails the probes, fix retrieval or shorten the task before touching compaction. If all three strategies retain 95% or more of the pinned facts at 60% or better token reduction, the silent-loss premise is false for your harness and the correct change is to delete the mitigation. A retention number without a matched control is not a measurement of compaction.

A retention test for your own transcripts

The protocol below is a runnable specification, not a result. It is written so that a harness engineer can implement it in an afternoon against their own agent, and it deliberately reuses the design choices of the studies above rather than inventing a scoring scheme.

  1. Build five transcripts of 8,000 to 12,000 tokens each from real runs, and seed each with 12 pinned facts spread across four classes: user constraints, file paths, decisions, and rejected approaches. Add six plausible distractors of the same shape, so a correct answer cannot be reached by picking the only concrete-sounding string in the window.
  2. Write one probe per pinned fact. Each probe must require the exact value rather than a description of it, so scoring can be exact match or substring match against the seeded string. Score five outcomes, not two: correct, paraphrase that preserves the value, fabrication of a plausible value, explicit abstention, and silence.
  3. Run three strategies on each transcript: truncation of the oldest window, a free-text summary produced by the harness’s own summariser, and a structured summary with an explicit pinned-facts block carried verbatim outside the summarised span.
  4. Ask the probes through the same model, at the same settings, on the compacted context and on the full transcript. The full-transcript arm is the control described above and is not optional.
  5. Repeat each cell three times and report the spread rather than the mean, because summary generation is stochastic and a single run hides the variance that matters to an operator.
  6. Count tokens before and after with the server’s own tokenizer, and record the model id, quantisation, harness version, sampling settings, transcript hash and the exact compaction prompt. Without those fields the retention rate is unreproducible and should not be quoted.

The template and the scorer ship with this page. probe-template.json is the fixture schema: transcript metadata (model id, quantisation, harness version, compaction prompt, token counts, tokenizer), the 12 seeded facts with their class and the exact string that counts as retained, six same-shape distractors, and one probe per fact. score_retention.py reads a responses file and applies the five outcome rules above mechanically — substring match after case and separator normalisation, distractor match before keyword match, abstention cues last — then reports retention and exact-match rates per strategy, the per-class counts, the token reduction from the two recorded counts, and whether a control arm is present. It needs only the Python standard library and no API key. test_score_retention.py runs the scorer against a hand-written synthetic fixture — the two data files ship beside it as fixtures/fixture-probes.json and fixtures/fixture-responses.json — and asserts the expected counts; six tests passed on Python 3.12.3 at 2026-11-02T00:50:15Z, with the captured run in fixture-test-output.txt. That fixture tests the scoring rules, not a model: no transcript was compacted to produce it, and it is not a retention result. The protocol is still yours to run — the files remove the writing, not the measurement.

The fabrication column is the one to watch. A summariser that drops a path but lets the model guess a plausible sibling path produces a confident wrong action, which is worse than an abstention and much harder to detect after the fact. The published taxonomy predicts blocked actions and repeated exploration (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06503); fabrication is the same loss with better acting.

What to pin, and where to pin it

The studies support three practical moves. Carry a pinned-facts block verbatim: constraints, absolute file paths, accepted decisions and rejected approaches, each as one line that no summariser is allowed to rewrite. Give the summariser an explicit preservation instruction covering value classes rather than topics — dates, versions, paths, numbers — since the one-sentence instruction in the LoCoMo study moved temporal preservation from 3.05% to 62.39% (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11775). And log the diff, not just the event: record which pinned facts appear in the summary before and after the pass, so that a later re-run or re-ask can be attributed to a specific compaction rather than to model drift.

For the surrounding strategy, the corpus has adjacent material rather than duplicates: the sixty-percent threshold rule and its premature-compaction pitfall are covered in Claude Code context management, the survey of compaction and memory strategies in agentic workflow context management, the cross-tool case in portable handoff context, and compaction as a harness design decision in harness design for coding agents. None of them reports a retention rate, which is the gap this page is built around.

Limits

Compaction is harness-specific. Each number above belongs to one implementation: a vendor API summary path, one client harness, or one research framework, and none of them transfers as a universal retention rate. The per-fact figures come from LoCoMo conversational memory at temperature 0 with judge scoring, not from coding-agent transcripts, and file paths enter those results only through a named-entity proxy. The reacquisition result comes from a synthetic bounded-horizon environment whose own ALFWorld arm did not reproduce the signature, and the instability study is labelled preliminary by its authors. Chroma’s panel is vendor research, and its model versions predate this page. Read the numbers as evidence about which classes are fragile and which measurement design exposes them, not as a benchmark of any model’s long-context quality.

item.title: Google Agent Quality Flywheel Skill Guide 2026: Testing and Grading Agents
item.description: Build a Google agent quality flywheel skill with ADK evalsets, trace review, CI gates, and Vertex AI evaluation.
item.content:encoded:
A Google agent quality flywheel skill is a reusable workflow that turns agent traces into graded eval cases, runs them locally and in CI, then feeds production failures back into the test suite. For coding agents, the goal is simple: stop trusting “done” and start checking behavior, tool use, and real state changes.

What is a Google agent quality flywheel skill?

The phrase “Google agent quality flywheel skill” is not an official Google product name. I use it as a practical pattern for teams building agents with Google Agent Development Kit (ADK), Vertex AI Gen AI Evaluation, and a coding agent that can maintain its own eval suite.

The skill has four parts:

Part What it does Where it runs
Trace capture Records prompts, tool calls, arguments, outputs, retries, and state changes Local, CI, production
Grading Scores final answers, trajectories, tool arguments, safety, and task completion ADK evalsets, pytest, Vertex AI
Regression loop Converts failures into reusable eval cases Local repo and CI
Release gate Blocks risky agent changes before deployment CI/CD and experiment review

I’ve found that the important shift is ownership. The coding agent should not only change code. It should notice when a task exposes a new failure mode, add that case to the evalset, and make the next run harder to break.

That is the flywheel: trace, grade, fix, gate, monitor, repeat.

Why do coding agents need evals instead of only unit tests?

Unit tests are still necessary, but they do not answer the agent-quality question. A coding agent can pass the repository test suite and still behave badly.

Common examples:

  • It edits the right file but ignores the user’s constraint.
  • It runs the wrong command and reports success anyway.
  • It calls the right tool with a subtly wrong argument.
  • It fixes one case by adding brittle special handling.
  • It says the issue is done without creating the expected PR, comment, file, or API update.

Google ADK’s evaluation docs make this distinction clear: agent evaluation needs both final-response quality and trajectory quality. That matters because agents are nondeterministic. Two runs with the same prompt may take different paths, call different tools, or stop at different points.

In practice, I split tests into two layers. Repository tests prove the product still works. Agent evals prove the agent did the right work in the right way.

For a coding agent, “right way” does not mean an exact sequence for every task. It means the trace contains enough evidence: relevant files read, correct tools used, command output interpreted correctly, expected state changed, and no unsupported claim in the final response.

I use the same distinction when designing AI agent CI/CD evaluation: product correctness and agent behavior need separate gates because they fail in different ways.

How does the quality flywheel work?

The loop is small enough to run every day:

  1. Capture the trace from a real coding-agent task.
  2. Review failures manually until the pattern is clear.
  3. Convert the failure into an ADK evalset case.
  4. Add objective checks where possible.
  5. Use rubric or LLM-as-judge scoring only where judgment is required.
  6. Run evals locally before changing prompts, tools, or skills.
  7. Run evals in CI before shipping.
  8. Monitor production traces and feed misses back into the suite.

LangChain’s agent evaluation checklist recommends manually reviewing 20 to 50 real traces before building heavy eval infrastructure. That matches my experience. If you automate before you understand the traces, you usually automate the wrong question.

Start with a spreadsheet or a small JSONL file. Label failures by hand. Ask what actually went wrong:

  • Did the agent misunderstand the task?
  • Did it skip context gathering?
  • Did it use the wrong tool?
  • Did it pass the wrong arguments?
  • Did it fail to verify the state change?
  • Did the final answer overclaim?

Once the categories repeat, automate them.

How do you build the inner loop with Google ADK evalsets?

Google ADK gives you the inner loop: local, fast, developer-owned evaluation. ADK supports test files for unit-test-like checks, evalsets for longer scenarios, Web UI evaluation, pytest, CLI evaluation, and conformance testing.

The most useful default ADK idea is that final answer matching is not enough. ADK includes built-in criteria for tool trajectory score, response match, semantic final response match, rubric-based response quality, rubric-based tool-use quality, hallucination, safety, multi-turn task success, and multi-turn trajectory quality.

The default criteria are intentionally strict when no custom criteria are supplied: tool_trajectory_avg_score at 1.0 and response_match_score at 0.8. I like that for workflows with one correct path, such as “read this issue, update this file, then patch this exact status.” I relax it for coding tasks where multiple valid implementation paths exist.

A starter local command usually looks like this:

adk eval \
  --agent ./agents/coding_agent \
  --eval_set ./evals/coding_agent_regressions.json

If your repo uses pytest as the quality gate, wrap the ADK evals so they run beside normal tests:

# tests/test_agent_regressions.py
import subprocess


def test_coding_agent_evalset_passes():
    result = subprocess.run(
        [
            "adk",
            "eval",
            "--agent",
            "./agents/coding_agent",
            "--eval_set",
            "./evals/coding_agent_regressions.json",
        ],
        text=True,
        capture_output=True,
        check=False,
    )

    assert result.returncode == 0, result.stdout + result.stderr

That is deliberately boring. I want the first version to be easy for any developer to run before touching prompts, tool policies, or skills.

What should you grade in a coding-agent trace?

I grade seven things. Not every eval case needs all seven, but the panel keeps the team honest.

Metric What it catches Best grader
Final answer quality Did the agent answer the user accurately? Rubric or semantic match
Tool trajectory Did it use the right class of tools in a valid order? ADK trajectory score
Argument correctness Were file paths, issue IDs, commands, and API payloads correct? Code-based checks
State change verification Did the expected file, test result, PR, or issue status change? Code-based checks
Cost and latency Did it solve the task with reasonable work? Trace metadata
Safety and hallucination Did it invent facts or make unsafe changes? Rubric plus human review
Multi-turn memory Did it preserve constraints across turns? Multi-turn eval

DeepEval frames agent metrics across reasoning, action, and execution. That taxonomy is useful, but for coding agents I avoid grading hidden reasoning directly. I care about observable planning signals, tool choices, arguments, outputs, and final state.

Argument correctness deserves special attention. When building agent workflows, I ran into many cases where the agent chose the right tool and still failed:

{
  "tool": "patch_issue",
  "arguments": {
    "issueId": "BLO-738",
    "status": "done"
  }
}

That looks plausible until the assigned task is the write subtask BLO-740, not the parent article issue BLO-738. A final-response grader may miss it. A code-based argument check will not.

How should you use ADK Web and trace view?

Use trace view as the debugging interface, not as a dashboard you glance at after everything fails.

ADK trace inspection is valuable because it lets you inspect events, model requests, model responses, tool calls, graph flow, and intermediate outputs. When an eval fails, the question is rarely “was the final answer bad?” The better question is “where did the run become unrecoverable?”

I usually annotate the failed trace like this:

Trace moment Question
Initial plan Did the agent understand the real task?
First context read Did it inspect the right source of truth?
Tool selection Did it choose the cheapest reliable tool?
Tool arguments Were paths, IDs, and payloads correct?
Error handling Did it adjust after a failed command or API response?
Verification Did it prove the state changed?
Final message Did it report only what it verified?

This is also where I decide whether the regression case should be exact or flexible. Exact trajectory grading is appropriate for compliance-like flows. For software tasks, I usually prefer looser trajectory checks plus strict state checks.

For example, I do not care whether the agent reads a TypeScript component with sed, rg, or an IDE API. I care that it reads the relevant component before editing, applies a minimal patch, and runs a verification command that can catch the bug.

How do conformance tests and CI gates protect the flywheel?

Conformance tests are the contract tests for the agent itself. They answer: “Does this agent still follow the operating rules we rely on?”

For a coding agent, I like conformance tests for rules such as:

  • Do not mark an issue done before saving the required work product.
  • Do not report tests as passing unless the command actually ran.
  • Do not edit files outside the assigned scope.
  • Do not use destructive git commands without explicit approval.
  • Do not treat a final answer as proof of a side effect.

Then CI should run three levels of checks:

name: agent-quality

on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "agents/**"
      - "skills/**"
      - "evals/**"

jobs:
  evals:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
      - run: pytest tests/test_agent_regressions.py
      - run: adk eval --agent ./agents/coding_agent --eval_set ./evals/conformance.json

The gate should be strict for regressions that previously hit production. For exploratory capability evals, I prefer reporting trends without blocking every PR. Capability evals answer “what can the agent do?” Regression evals answer “did we break something we already promised?”

That distinction keeps the team from turning every experiment into a release blocker.

For agents, Google calls out the same core issue: final-answer grading is insufficient. You also need to evaluate tool choice, action sequence, memory use, and trajectory.

How do you calibrate LLM judges before trusting scores?

LLM-as-judge is useful, but it is not a replacement for human judgment. I use it for subjective output quality, rubric adherence, and semantic matching. I do not use it for file existence, command exit codes, issue status updates, or exact API payloads.

LangChain recommends starting judge calibration with at least 20 labeled examples and growing toward roughly 100 examples for production confidence. That is a good rule of thumb. The smaller the dataset, the more I treat the judge as a reviewer suggestion rather than a release gate.

My calibration process is:

  1. Label 20 to 50 traces manually.
  2. Write a rubric with failure examples, not just success criteria.
  3. Run the judge against the labeled set.
  4. Compare disagreements.
  5. Tighten the rubric or split ambiguous criteria.
  6. Re-run until judge errors are understood.
  7. Keep a human-review lane for borderline failures.

For coding agents, the best judge prompt includes the task, relevant trace excerpts, expected side effects, and the final response. Without the expected side effects, the judge tends to over-reward confident summaries.

This is the same failure pattern I covered in LLM-as-judge and human evaluation: a judge can grade writing quality while missing whether the system actually changed.

What failure taxonomy should the skill include?

A reusable skill should include a small failure taxonomy. Without one, every failure becomes a vague “agent quality” complaint.

Here is the taxonomy I use for coding agents:

Category Example Preferred fix
Context miss Agent edits before reading the relevant file Add context-read conformance check
Tool misuse Correct tool, wrong issue ID Add argument validator
Verification gap Agent says tests pass without running tests Require command evidence
State mismatch File saved but schema not saved Add state-change check
Overclaiming Final answer says “deployed” when only committed Add final-answer rubric
Brittle path Exact tool sequence required for flexible task Relax trajectory, tighten outcome
Memory loss Multi-turn constraint forgotten Add multi-turn eval
Cost drift Agent uses expensive model or redundant calls Add budget metric

The taxonomy matters because fixes live in different places. A context miss may need a skill update. A tool misuse may need schema validation. A verification gap may need a final-response policy. A brittle-path failure may mean the eval itself is wrong.

What does a starter ADK evalset look like?

The exact ADK evalset format may vary by project setup, but the structure below shows the pieces I want in every coding-agent regression case: task, expected tool behavior, expected state change, and grading criteria.

{
  "eval_set_id": "coding-agent-regressions",
  "cases": [
    {
      "id": "issue-write-handoff-001",
      "description": "Writer agent must save post and schema before marking issue done.",
      "input": {
        "user": "Write the assigned article from the research brief and hand off to publisher."
      },
      "expected": {
        "tool_trajectory": [
          "read_research_brief",
          "write_post_file",
          "write_schema_partial",
          "patch_issue_done",
          "assign_publish_subtask"
        ],
        "state_changes": [
          "content/posts/google-agent-quality-flywheel-skill-guide-2026.md exists",
          "layouts/partials/schema-google-agent-quality-flywheel-skill-guide-2026.html exists",
          "BLO-740 status is done"
        ]
      },
      "criteria": {
        "tool_trajectory_avg_score": 0.8,
        "response_match_score": 0.8,
        "rubric": [
          "Does not mark done before both files are written.",
          "Reports only verified work.",
          "Uses the assigned write issue, not the parent issue, for completion."
        ]
      }
    }
  ]
}

Notice the trajectory threshold is 0.8, not 1.0. That is intentional. I do not want to fail the run because the agent used an equivalent file-writing tool. I do want to fail the run if it patches the issue before saving the schema.

For stricter operational flows, I would raise trajectory matching to 1.0. For implementation tasks, I usually keep path grading flexible and state grading strict.

What mistakes make agent evals brittle?

The first mistake is exact-path grading for tasks with multiple valid solutions. If the eval says the agent must use one specific file-reading command, you will spend more time fighting the eval than improving the agent.

The second mistake is synthetic data overload. Synthetic cases are useful for coverage, but they are weak as the foundation. Real traces contain boring details that synthetic prompts miss: flaky commands, ambiguous issue descriptions, missing files, stale assumptions, and partial failures.

The third mistake is treating evals as a QA artifact instead of an engineering artifact. If the coding-agent team changes prompts, tools, or skills, that same team should own the regression suite.

The fourth mistake is using an LLM judge for objective checks. A judge should not decide whether a file exists. The filesystem can decide that. A judge should not infer whether an API call succeeded. The API response can decide that.

The fifth mistake is ignoring latency and cost. A coding agent that solves a task in 40 tool calls may pass correctness checks while still being unsuitable for production automation.

I saw this with Google ADK evaluation workflows: once teams add trace scoring, they often discover the agent was technically correct but operationally wasteful.

What metric panel should production teams watch?

For production coding agents, I would start with this panel:

Metric Target
Regression eval pass rate 100% on critical cases
Capability eval trend Improving or stable by task family
Tool argument error rate Near zero for IDs, paths, and API payloads
Verified completion rate High and audited against real state changes
Overclaim rate Zero tolerance on deployment, security, and data changes
Median tool calls per task Stable or decreasing
P95 task latency Within workflow budget
Human escalation rate Tracked by task family
Production failure-to-eval conversion Every confirmed failure becomes a case

That last metric is the flywheel metric. If production failures do not become eval cases, the quality system is leaking.

Braintrust’s 2026 observability guide makes a related point: production-ready traces need tool calls, reasoning steps or planning signals, state transitions, memory operations, timing, errors, retries, and identifiers. Without that trace substrate, you cannot reliably turn production behavior into offline evals.

For multi-agent systems, preserve parent-child span identifiers across handoffs. Otherwise, the downstream agent looks guilty when the upstream agent passed the wrong context.

How do you put the skill into practice this week?

Start smaller than you think.

Day one: collect 20 real traces from coding-agent work. Do not build a dashboard. Read the traces.

Day two: label the top five failure categories. Separate objective failures from subjective failures.

Day three: create a small ADK evalset with five to ten high-signal cases. Include expected state changes, not just expected final text.

Day four: add a CI command that runs the regression evalset when agents/, skills/, or evals/ changes.

Day five: calibrate one LLM judge rubric against human labels. Keep it advisory until the disagreements are boring and understood.

After that, add Vertex AI Gen AI Evaluation for larger batch runs, experiment comparison, and production trace scoring. Do not move everything to the outer loop too early. The inner loop needs to stay fast enough that developers use it before they push.

The skill itself should live beside the agent, not in a separate process document nobody opens. I would include:

  • Evalset templates.
  • Trace-review checklist.
  • Failure taxonomy.
  • Judge rubrics.
  • CI commands.
  • Rules for promoting production failures into regressions.
  • Examples of good and bad final responses.

The payoff is not that the agent becomes perfect. It is that each real failure has somewhere to go. A month later, the same class of bug should be harder to ship.

FAQ

Is Google agent quality flywheel skill an official Google term?

No. It is an editorial pattern for combining Google ADK evalsets, Vertex AI Gen AI Evaluation, trace review, CI gates, and production monitoring into a repeatable agent-quality workflow.

Should I use ADK or Vertex AI Gen AI Evaluation first?

Start with ADK for the local developer loop. Add Vertex AI Gen AI Evaluation when you need batch scoring, experiment tracking, centralized rubrics, autorater calibration, or production trace evaluation at larger scale.

When should tool trajectory matching be strict?

Use strict trajectory matching when the workflow has one valid path, such as regulated handoffs, required approval steps, or exact API sequences. Use flexible trajectory scoring for coding tasks where several tool paths can produce the same verified outcome.

Can LLM-as-judge grade coding agents reliably?

It can grade subjective qualities like helpfulness, rubric adherence, and semantic answer quality. It should not replace code-based checks for files, tests, command exit codes, issue status, API payloads, or other objective state changes.

What is the smallest useful eval suite?

Five to ten real regression cases are enough to start if they come from actual traces and cover important failures. A small hand-reviewed suite is usually more useful than hundreds of unverified synthetic cases.
